questions.whenWhy: Where the bytes travel is the storage design the plan reverses. It decides privacy and the free tier.
questions.recWhy: The plan promises that no document byte touches our servers, and today the server reads the whole repository with our own token: it downloads the zipball, unzips it and parses every file on our side. Reading file by file from the browser cannot replace that, because a 5,832-file vault is 5,833 calls against GitHub's 5,000 an hour limit, and the repo scan the pilot depends on reads every file. One tarball request is the only whole-vault read that sits inside the limit and spares our server, so the browser fetches the tarball and unzips it in the page. Two things are unmeasured and both are cheap to test before a line is written: whether a browser can follow GitHub's zipball redirect, and whether 88.1 MB of markdown in a tab is survivable. Q9 carries this as the first item of the privacy block. Either test failing sends this to per-file reading with a published ceiling.

questions.recWhy: Review state, what you have read, is a file in the repository, so on the web every review action is a git write, and nothing in the plan says when that write happens. Marks come far faster than edits: one commit per mark floods the history with commits the user did not make and spends the same 5,000 an hour budget the reads need. Batching on idle, file close and tab close gives one commit a session that still lands in the repository; a killed tab loses that session's marks and two machines can disagree for a session. (d) forfeits the one claim nothing else in the market reaches, durable across machines. E37 decides how two people's review files merge and E36 how a record survives a rename; this card is the third leg. It sits after the pilot because Q6 makes the instruction-file view read-only first. Short-burst reviewing that loses marks to closed tabs sends this to (a).

Every model provider behaves differently, so supporting the user's choice is support cost that never ends.

questions.recWhy: Nothing in the tools checked on 13 September offers generation on a key the user holds, so offline with your own key is the one feature here that nothing in the comparison set has. A key the user holds costs us no model spend, no metering and no ceiling, three things that are not built, and it keeps the privacy claim exact, which is the part a competitor cannot copy cheaply. AC13 is the web half of the same question and lands the same way. One provider at first, because every provider behaves differently and supporting the user's choice is support cost that never ends. This sits after the pilot because Q3 has the desktop surface arriving later and Q10 already settles the key. questions.whenWhy: Repository access is the riskiest item on the list and it reopens `L1`, so it is last rather than planned.
questions.q: If we ever read a user's repository, is it read only, and is writing ruled out in writing?
questions.lede: Reading a repository to write better documents about it is a different proposition, legally and commercially, from writing to it.
questions.stakes: Writing to a customer's repository makes us an intermediary holding their code, with every duty `L1` costs at 74 founder hours.
state: The direction given on 13 September proposes connecting GitHub and the local machine on the top plan.
`L1` prices the intermediary duties that holding customer content brings.
Claude Code, Cursor and Codex already run on the local machine and do this well.
tension: A kit written with the repository in view is far better than one written from answers alone.
Every byte of customer code we touch is a duty, and the value is nearly all on the reading side.

costs: Users will ask for write and we will keep refusing

options.screens: A connect screen naming the scope.
options.what: Read only, forever, written into the operating rules. Most of the value at a fraction of the duty and a claim write-access tools cannot make; users will ask for write and we keep refusing.

No transit duty at all

recCase: Nearly all the value of repository access is on the reading side, and nearly all the duty is on the writing side.
Ruling writing out in the operating rules turns a refusal into a claim, which is how this product argues everywhere else.

questions.recWhy: Reading a repository to write better documents about it is a different proposition, legally and commercially, from writing to it. Nearly all the value of repository access is on the reading side, a kit written with the code in view is far better than one written from answers, and nearly all the duty is on the writing side: every byte we write into customer code is L1's intermediary duty arriving at once, against Claude Code, Cursor and Codex, which already do this well on the local machine. Ruling writing out in the operating rules turns a refusal into a claim, which is how this product argues everywhere. It is also why AC3 keeps three permissions though Q2 settled the buyer as the team. It sits after the pilot because the top plan that connects GitHub is Q13's team tier and comes later. If users will not paste and will not connect a read-only token either, (c) is the honest fallback.
